books.section: A. The Chesapeake and the Upper South

options.misconception: Tobacco needed large tracts — the table's millions of pounds came from spreading out, not from small plots.

rationales.A: Tobacco needed large tracts — the table's millions of pounds came from spreading out, not from small plots.
rationales.B: Tobacco was labor-intensive — that is why the region turned to indentured servants and enslaved workers.
rationales.C: Background: tobacco wore out the soil after a few years, so planters had to keep opening new fields, and each new field needed hands — which is why the region imported servants and enslaved workers.
rationales.D: The land went to tobacco fields, not towns — the Chesapeake built few towns at all.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the scale. Thirty-five million pounds a year is not a garden crop — it is an industry.
2. Add the background. Tobacco drained the soil in a few years, so a planter's fields were always wearing out.
3. Put the two together. More tobacco meant more new land, and more new land meant more workers.
Remember: a crop that eats its own soil makes its growers hungry for land — and for labor.
